glossary.Epithelial cells: Cells that line surfaces and ducts; most breast cancers start in the duct lining.
glossary.Heterozygous: Carrying one faulty copy and one normal copy of a gene.
glossary.Relative risk: How many times more likely an outcome is in one group than another.
glossary.Oestrogen exposure: Total lifetime exposure of breast tissue to oestrogen; more exposure means more risk.
glossary.Late menopause: Periods stopping later than usual, giving more years of oestrogen exposure.
glossary.Asymmetry: One breast looking different in size or shape from the other.
glossary.Nipple discharge: Fluid leaking from the nipple; bloody or one-sided discharge needs assessment.
glossary.Axillary lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes in the armpit.
glossary.Ducts: The tubes that carry milk from the lobules to the nipple.
glossary.Lobules: The milk-producing glands of the breast.
glossary.Incidental: Found by chance while looking for something else.
glossary.Benign: Not cancer; does not invade or spread.
glossary.Chest wall: The ribs, muscles and tissues of the chest under the breast.
glossary.Metastasis: Spread of cancer from where it started to distant sites.
glossary.Screening: Testing healthy people with no symptoms to find disease early.
glossary.Dense breast tissue: Breast with more glandular tissue, common in younger women, which hides lesions on mammograms.
glossary.Ultrasound: Imaging with sound waves; used first in under-40s with dense breasts.
glossary.PET scan: Imaging with a radioactive glucose tracer that lights up active cancer, used for metastases.
glossary.Axillary ultrasound: Ultrasound of the armpit to look for involved lymph nodes before surgery.
glossary.Peripheral: Away from the centre, here away from the nipple.
glossary.Radiotherapy: Treatment using high-energy radiation to kill cancer cells.
glossary.Residual margins: Cancer cells left at the cut edge of removed tissue.
glossary.Fluorouracil: A chemotherapy drug that blocks DNA synthesis; the F in FEC-D.
glossary.Epirubicin: An anthracycline chemotherapy drug; the E in FEC-D.
glossary.Docetaxel: A taxane chemotherapy drug that stops cell division; the D in FEC-D.
glossary.Node-positive: Cancer has spread to the lymph nodes.
glossary.Herceptin: Brand name for trastuzumab, the anti-HER2 antibody.
glossary.Heart failure: The heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs.
glossary.Perimenopausal: The years around the menopause when periods become irregular.
glossary.Hot flushes: Sudden feelings of heat and sweating, a side effect of tamoxifen.
glossary.BMD: Bone mineral density, measured by DEXA; falls on aromatase inhibitors.
glossary.Osteoporosis: Thin, fragile bones with a high fracture risk.
glossary.Brain metastases: Cancer that has spread to the brain, causing headache, seizures or focal deficits.
glossary.Palliative: Treatment aimed at relieving symptoms rather than cure.
glossary.Tumour suppressor genes: Genes that normally stop cells growing out of control; loss of both copies allows cancer.
glossary.Double-strand break: A break across both strands of DNA, repaired by BRCA-dependent pathways.
glossary.Loss-of-function: A mutation that stops a gene's protein working.
glossary.Overexpression: Making far more of a protein than normal.
glossary.Cutaneous oedema: Swelling of the skin from trapped fluid.
glossary.Sentinel node: The first lymph node that drains a tumour, so the first to receive spreading cells.
